abstract: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. We anticipate that GinsengMind will facilitate research on medicinal plant specialized metabolism, natural product biosynthesis, enzyme discovery and engineering, and synthetic biology, while offering an adaptable framework for developing domain-specialized AI research agents across other medicinal plants and scientific disciplines.
